title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store
summary: You'll be able to design a Dynamo-style key-value store from the building blocks you've learned: consistent hashing, replication, N/R/W quorums, vector clocks, hinted handoff, gossip, Merkle trees and LSM storage.

questions.prompt: In a leaderless key-value store, what do **N**, **R** and **W** mean, and why does `R + W > N` matter?
questions.hint: Draw 3 replicas and shade which ones a write touched and which ones a read asked.
keyPoints: N is the number of replicas of each key; W is how many must acknowledge a write; R is how many must answer a read
If R + W > N, any read set and any write set share at least one replica, so a read can see the latest acknowledged write
Example: N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 tolerates one unavailable replica for both reads and writes
Lower R or W means lower latency and higher availability but weaker consistency (e.g. R = W = 1 is eventual consistency)
Caveat: sloppy quorums and concurrent writes mean it is not full linearizability

questions.prompt: Each replica is independently available **99.5%** of the time and N = 3. Compute the probability that a write succeeds with **W = 3**, **W = 2** and **W = 1**. What does the result say about requiring every replica to acknowledge?
questions.hint: P(at least 2 of 3 up) = p³ + 3p²(1 − p).
keyPoints: Requiring all replicas makes the system less available than a single node (98.5% < 99.5%)
Quorums give both overlap (with a matching R) and high availability; assumes independent failures

questions.prompt: Write `compareClocks(a, b)` for vector clocks given as objects like `{ A: 2, B: 1 }` (a missing node counts as 0). Return `"equal"`, `"a-after-b"`, `"b-after-a"` or `"concurrent"`. Then write `resolve(versions)` that takes an array of `{ value, clock }` and returns only the versions **not dominated** by another version (the siblings to keep).
questions.hint: Check every node in the union of both clocks; track whether either side was ever strictly bigger.
keyPoints: Iterates over the union of node IDs, treating missing entries as 0
Concurrent when each clock has at least one larger counter; ordered when only one side is ever larger; equal when neither
resolve drops any version whose clock happened before another version's clock
resolve also removes exact duplicates (equal clocks) so a sibling isn't returned twice
Returns more than one version only for truly concurrent writes

questions.prompt: Replica node D goes down for **10 minutes** during heavy writes, then comes back. A week later, another node's disk dies and it is replaced with an empty machine. Explain how the store keeps accepting writes and how each node gets its missing data back.
questions.hint: Short outage: sticky notes. Long or total loss: compare inventories efficiently.
keyPoints: During D's outage, writes for D's keys go to the next healthy node with a hint (sloppy quorum), so W acks are still reached
Gossip/failure detection notices D is back, and hint holders hand off the writes, then delete them (hinted handoff)
Reads that see a stale replica trigger read repair, fixing frequently read keys
For the replaced empty node, anti-entropy streams its key ranges from other replicas, using Merkle trees to compare ranges cheaply and transfer only differing buckets
Merkle trees let replicas compare via root hashes and descend only into differing subtrees (about log(buckets) levels)

questions.prompt:
Size the cluster: **4 billion** keys with **2 KB** average values, N = 3. Nodes have **8 TB** disks that you keep at most **50%** full. Traffic is **300k reads/s** at R = 2 and **150k writes/s** sent to all N replicas. One node handles **40k replica operations/s**.

How many nodes for storage, how many for throughput, and what do you provision?
questions.hint: Compute both and take the larger, then add headroom.
keyPoints: Data = 4e9 × 2 KB = 8 TB; × 3 replicas = 24 TB
Usable per node = 4 TB → 24 / 4 = 6 nodes for storage
Throughput dominates; provision ~32–40 nodes for failure and growth headroom, spread across zones
Notes that compaction, repair and rebalancing also need spare capacity
questions.answer:
```text
Storage:    4e9 × 2 KB = 8 TB × 3 = 24 TB; 24 TB / 4 TB usable = 6 nodes
Throughput: 300k × 2 + 150k × 3 = 1.05M replica ops/s; 1.05M / 40k ≈ 26.3 → 27 nodes
Provision:  throughput wins → ~27 + ~30% headroom ≈ 35 nodes
```

questions.prompt: Two teams want to use your store. Team A stores **shopping carts**; Team B stores **account balances**. For each, recommend N/R/W and a conflict-resolution strategy, and explain whether your Dynamo-style store is the right tool at all.
questions.hint: What is the cost of losing a write, versus the cost of rejecting one?
keyPoints: Carts value availability: e.g. N = 3, W = 2 (or 1), R = 2 with sloppy quorums so adds always succeed
For carts, keep concurrent versions as siblings and merge by union (an added item is never lost; a removed item may reappear, which is acceptable)
Last-write-wins would silently drop concurrent cart updates, so avoid it there
Balances need strong consistency and atomic read-modify-write; leaderless quorums with LWW can lose updates or double-spend
Recommend a strongly consistent system for balances (single-leader/consensus-based DB with transactions, or a ledger as on Day 65), not the AP store
Frames the choice as CAP/PACELC: availability and latency vs consistency
